common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Treats mass and weight as the same number with the unit swapped, so the factor $g$ is dropped from $mg\Delta h$ as well.
Has the relationship upside down; weight is mass multiplied by $g$, not divided.
Does the arithmetic correctly but keeps the unit of mass, so weight is not yet being treated as a force.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks that mass in kilograms and weight in newtons are kept apart, because $mg$ in $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$ is exactly the weight of the object.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Write mass, $g$ and weight in a three-column line for two or three objects, saying the unit out loud each time, before using $mg\Delta h$.

diagnostic_items.question: Without a calculator, work out $0.50^2$ and $3.0^2$.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Doubles instead of squaring, so every $v^2$ will be wrong by a large factor.
Misplaces the decimal point: $0.50^2=0.25$, which is half of 0.50, whereas 0.025 is one twentieth of 0.50.
Again multiplies by 2 rather than by itself.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks the one piece of arithmetic that $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$ depends on; an error in $v^2$ carries straight through into the energy.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Rewrite each square as an explicit multiplication, $0.50\times0.50$ and $3.0\times3.0$, and compare the answer with the original number to see whether it should have grown or shrunk.

diagnostic_items.question: A cyclist travels $120\,\mathrm{m}$ in $15\,\mathrm{s}$. What speed should be put into $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$, and in what unit?
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: $v=120\,\mathrm{m}\div15\,\mathrm{s}=8.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The single number $8.0$, in metres per second, is what goes into the equation.

common_wrong_answers.interpretation: Uses distance in place of speed, so the time is never brought in and the unit is wrong.
Divides the wrong way round; speed is distance per unit time, not time per unit distance.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks that speed is already handled as one measured quantity in m/s, rather than as a distance and a time kept separate.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Calculate two or three speeds from distance and time, writing the unit m/s each time, before any kinetic energy is calculated.

theory_blocks.title: More speed, more height: more energy, but not always by the same amount
theory_blocks.body:
You already know that a moving object holds energy in its kinetic store, and a raised object holds energy in its gravitational potential store.

A faster car clearly holds more kinetic energy than a slow one, and a book on a high shelf clearly holds more gravitational potential energy than the same book on the floor.

What is not obvious just from that general idea is exactly how much more. Does doubling a car's speed double its kinetic energy? Does doubling a shelf's height double a common textbook's gravitational potential energy?

[[blue:This lesson answers both questions precisely, with two equations, and the two answers turn out to be different from each other.]]

theory_blocks.title: Kinetic energy: Ek = ½mv²
theory_blocks.body:
The kinetic energy of a moving object is

$$E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$$

with mass $m$ in kilograms, speed $v$ in metres per second, and $E_k$ in joules. Notice that $v$ is squared, not just multiplied by $m$: this is the single most important feature of the equation,

and the direct cause of the doubling-speed result in the next block.

This equation applies to any object with mass that is moving at the stated speed; it does not distinguish direction, so the same equation gives the same $E_k$ whether the object moves left, right, up or down.

theory_blocks.title: Why doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy
theory_blocks.body:
Because $E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$ depends on $v^2$, scaling the speed by some factor scales the kinetic energy by that factor **squared**, not by the factor itself.

Doubling the speed ($\times 2$) multiplies $E_k$ by $2^2=4$. Tripling the speed ($\times 3$) multiplies $E_k$ by $3^2=9$. Halving the speed divides $E_k$ by $2^2=4$, not by 2.

For a $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object, going from $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ changes $E_k$ from $4.0\,\mathrm{J}$ to $16.0\,\mathrm{J}$: four times as much, from only twice the speed.

theory_blocks.title: Gravitational potential energy: ΔEp = mgΔh
theory_blocks.body:
The change in gravitational potential energy when an object's height changes is

$$\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$$

with mass $m$ in kilograms, gravitational field strength $g$ in N/kg (take $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ throughout this course), vertical height change $\Delta h$ in metres, and $\Delta E_p$ in joules.

Since $mg$ is the object's weight in newtons, this is really (weight) $\times$ (vertical height change), matching the work equation $W=Fd$ from the previous lesson,

with the weight acting as the force and $\Delta h$ as the distance moved along that force's own (vertical) direction.

theory_blocks.title: Δh is the vertical height gained, never the slope length
theory_blocks.body:
A common trap is using the length of a ramp, hill or staircase in place of $\Delta h$. The equation only ever uses the [[blue:**vertical** height gained]], measured straight up,

because that is the distance moved along the direction of the object's weight (a vertical force), exactly as the work equation requires.

In the figure below, an object moves $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ up a slope, but the vertical height it actually gains is only $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ (with a $4.0\,\mathrm{m}$ horizontal base, forming a $3\text{-}4\text{-}5$ right triangle: $3.0^2+4.0^2=5.0^2$).

A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object moving up this slope gains $\Delta E_p=2.0\times9.8\times3.0=58.8\,\mathrm{J}$, using $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$, not $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$.

assets.caption: An object moves 5.0 m up a slope, but the vertical height it gains is only 3.0 m (a 3-4-5 right triangle: $3.0^2+4.0^2=5.0^2$). Only this 3.0 m enters ΔEp = mgΔh.
assets.purpose: Make the distinction between slope length and vertical height visually explicit, with a geometrically verified right triangle and the vertical height marked in red as the quantity that counts.

theory_blocks.title: Kinetic and gravitational energy can exchange, with the total conserved
theory_blocks.body:
A falling or swinging object continually exchanges gravitational potential energy for kinetic energy (or back again), while the total of the two stays constant if nothing else is involved.

As an object falls through a height $\Delta h$ with negligible air resistance, the gravitational potential energy it loses, $mg\Delta h$, equals the kinetic energy it gains, $\tfrac12 mv^2$.

Setting these equal, $mg\Delta h=\tfrac12 mv^2$, lets you find the speed at the bottom of a fall directly from the height, without needing to know the time taken.

keywords.definition: The energy a moving object has, calculated as $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$.
The energy an object has because of its height above a reference level; its change is calculated as $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$.
The quantity $g$, measured in N/kg, giving the weight per kilogram of mass; taken as $9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ in this course.
The height gained measured straight up, used in $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$; distinct from the length of any sloped or curved path taken.
The feature of $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$ whereby kinetic energy scales with the square of the speed, so scaling the speed by a factor scales $E_k$ by that factor squared.

worked_examples.statement: **A rolling ball.** A ball of mass $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ moves at $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Calculate its kinetic energy.
reasoning: Apply $E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$.
Square the speed before multiplying by mass and by one-half.
worked_examples.solution: $E_k=\tfrac12\times1.0\times4.0^2=\tfrac12\times1.0\times16=8.0\,\mathrm{J}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Squaring the speed first ($4.0^2=16$) before applying the other factors avoids the common error of multiplying $m$, $v$ and $\tfrac12$ in the wrong order.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Calculating $\tfrac12\times1.0\times4.0=2.0\,\mathrm{J}$ by forgetting to square the speed.

worked_examples.statement: **Lifting a crate.** A crate of mass $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ is raised $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$ vertically. Calculate the change in its gravitational potential energy.
reasoning: Apply $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$.
Multiply the three quantities together, keeping $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ throughout.
worked_examples.solution: $\Delta E_p=4.0\times9.8\times2.0=78.4\,\mathrm{J}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: This 78.4 J matches the work done by whatever lifted the crate, since lifting at constant speed means the lifting force equals the crate's weight.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N}$ instead of $9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, which does not affect the number here but breaks the unit reasoning behind the formula.

worked_examples.statement: **Doubling the speed.** A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object speeds up from $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, exactly doubling its speed. Calculate its kinetic energy at both speeds, and state the factor by which the kinetic energy has changed.
reasoning: Calculate each kinetic energy separately from the formula, rather than assuming how it scales.
Divide the second value by the first to find the actual factor of change.
worked_examples.solution: $E_{k1}=\tfrac12\times2.0\times2.0^2=4.0\,\mathrm{J}$. $E_{k2}=\tfrac12\times2.0\times4.0^2=16.0\,\mathrm{J}$. The kinetic energy has increased by a factor of $16.0/4.0=4$, not by a factor of 2.
worked_examples.interpretation: Doubling the speed ($\times2$) quadruples the kinetic energy ($\times2^2=\times4$), because $v$ is squared in the formula.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming that because the speed doubled, the kinetic energy must also have simply doubled, to $8.0\,\mathrm{J}$.

worked_examples.statement: **From motion to height.** A ball of mass $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ moves at $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ along the ground. (a) Calculate its kinetic energy. (b) The ball is then thrown and rises to a height of $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ above the ground before momentarily stopping. Calculate the gravitational potential energy it has gained at that height, relative to the ground.
reasoning: Apply $E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$ for part (a), using the given speed.
Apply $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$ for part (b), using the given vertical height.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $E_k=\tfrac12\times2.0\times3.0^2=9.0\,\mathrm{J}$. (b) $\Delta E_p=2.0\times9.8\times5.0=98\,\mathrm{J}$.
worked_examples.interpretation:
The two calculations use different formulas for different stores, and there is no requirement here that the two values be equal;

this ball's initial 9.0 J of kinetic energy on the ground is a separate quantity from the 98 J it later gains in height once something else (a throw) has acted on it.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the two answers must match, or using the speed in the height formula (or vice versa) by mixing up which equation applies.

guided_exercises.statement: A trolley of mass $3.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ moves at $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Calculate its kinetic energy.
hints: Write down $E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$ before substituting any numbers.
Square the speed first.
Multiply by the mass, then by one-half.
common_errors: Writing $\tfrac12\times3.0\times2.0=3.0\,\mathrm{J}$ by forgetting to square the speed.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Write down $E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$ before substituting any numbers.

**Step 2 — Method:** Square the speed first.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $E_k=\tfrac12\times3.0\times2.0^2=6.0\,\mathrm{J}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Multiply by the mass, then by one-half.

guided_exercises.statement: A $5.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ box is lifted $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$ vertically onto a shelf. Calculate the change in its gravitational potential energy.
hints: Write down $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$ before substituting.
Use $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.
Multiply all three quantities together.
common_errors: Leaving out $g$ entirely and calculating $5.0\times3.0=15\,\mathrm{J}$.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Write down $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$ before substituting.

**Step 2 — Method:** Use $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $\Delta E_p=5.0\times9.8\times3.0=147\,\mathrm{J}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Multiply all three quantities together.

exercises.statement: A $0.20\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball moves at $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Calculate its kinetic energy.
exercises.answer: $E_k=\tfrac12\times0.20\times10.0^2=10.0\,\mathrm{J}$.

exercises.statement: A $12.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ sack of cement is lifted $1.5\,\mathrm{m}$ vertically onto a pallet. Calculate the change in its gravitational potential energy.
exercises.answer: $\Delta E_p=12.0\times9.8\times1.5=176.4\,\mathrm{J}$.
exercises.full_solution: Multiplying in order: $12.0\times9.8=117.6$, then $117.6\times1.5=176.4\,\mathrm{J}$.

exercises.statement: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ crate is dragged up the slope shown in the lesson's figure: $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ along the slope, gaining a vertical height of $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$. Calculate the change in the crate's gravitational potential energy, stating clearly which of the two distances you use and why.
exercises.answer: $\Delta E_p=2.0\times9.8\times3.0=58.8\,\mathrm{J}$, using the vertical height ($3.0\,\mathrm{m}$), not the $5.0\,\mathrm{m}$ slope length.
exercises.full_solution: Only the vertical component of the motion is along the direction of the crate's weight, so only that 3.0 m enters mgΔh; the 5.0 m slope length is not used in this formula at all.

exercises.statement: A $0.50\,\mathrm{kg}$ stone is dropped from a height of $2.0\,\mathrm{m}$, with air resistance negligible. Using the idea that gravitational potential energy lost equals kinetic energy gained, calculate the stone's speed just before it lands.
exercises.answer: $\Delta E_p=0.50\times9.8\times2.0=9.8\,\mathrm{J}$, so $\tfrac12\times0.50\times v^2=9.8$, giving $v^2=39.2$ and $v\approx6.3\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
exercises.full_solution: Setting the lost gravitational potential energy equal to the gained kinetic energy ($mg\Delta h=\tfrac12mv^2$) and rearranging for $v$ gives a speed without ever needing the time of fall.

exam_questions.statement: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object moves at $5.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (a) Calculate its kinetic energy. (b) Its speed then doubles to $10.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Calculate its new kinetic energy, and state the factor by which the kinetic energy has increased.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $E_k=\tfrac12\times2.0\times5.0^2=25.0\,\mathrm{J}$. (b) $E_k=\tfrac12\times2.0\times10.0^2=100.0\,\mathrm{J}$, an increase by a factor of $100.0/25.0=4$.
exam_questions.full_solution: The speed doubled, and the kinetic energy increased by $2^2=4$, consistent with $E_k\propto v^2$.
mark_scheme: Calculates $E_k=25.0\,\mathrm{J}$ for part (a).
Calculates $E_k=100.0\,\mathrm{J}$ for part (b).
States the factor of increase as 4.
Links the factor of 4 to the speed being squared in the formula.
common_errors: Stating the kinetic energy has doubled (to 50 J) because the speed doubled.

exam_questions.statement: A $60\,\mathrm{kg}$ person climbs a vertical ladder, gaining a height of $3.0\,\mathrm{m}$. (a) Calculate the change in their gravitational potential energy. (b) Name the transfer pathway responsible for this energy change, and state which energy store loses energy to supply it.
exam_questions.answer: (a) $\Delta E_p=60\times9.8\times3.0=1764\,\mathrm{J}$. (b) The pathway is mechanical work (the person's leg muscles exert an upward force through the vertical height climbed); the energy comes from the chemical store in the person's muscles, built up from food.
exam_questions.full_solution: (a) $\Delta E_p=60\times9.8\times3.0=1764\,\mathrm{J}$. (b) The pathway is mechanical work (the person's leg muscles exert an upward force through the vertical height climbed); the energy comes from the chemical store in the person's muscles, built up from food.
mark_scheme: (a) M1 for substituting $\Delta E_p=60\times9.8\times3.0$; A1 for $1764\,\mathrm{J}$ (accept $1760\,\mathrm{J}$ or $1.8\,\mathrm{kJ}$) with correct unit.
Names the pathway as mechanical work.
Identifies the chemical energy store (in the muscles, from food) as the source.
common_errors: Leaving part (b) blank, or naming 'energy' generically instead of identifying the specific store and pathway.

challenge_questions.statement: An $800\,\mathrm{kg}$ car travels at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. (a) Calculate its kinetic energy. (b) Find the vertical height to which the same car would have to be raised to gain exactly this much gravitational potential energy, giving your answer to 2 significant figures.
hints: Calculate the kinetic energy first, from $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$.
Set $mg\Delta h$ equal to that kinetic energy and rearrange for $\Delta h$.
Keep full precision until the final answer, then round to 2 significant figures.
challenge_questions.full_solution: This combines both equations from the lesson: the same numeric energy value is reached either by a car's motion or by lifting the same car about 20 m into the air, showing the two stores really are measured on the same joule scale.

mcq.stem: A $4.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object moves at $3.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its kinetic energy?

options.why_wrong: leaves out the factor of one-half, calculating $4.0\times3.0^2$ without halving it.
forgets to square the speed, calculating $\tfrac12\times4.0\times3.0$ instead.
leaves out both the square and the one-half, calculating $4.0\times3.0$ alone.

mcq.explanation: $E_k=\tfrac12\times4.0\times3.0^2=\tfrac12\times4.0\times9.0=18\,\mathrm{J}$.

mcq.stem: A $1.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object's speed increases from $2.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to $4.0\,\mathrm{m/s}$, doubling. What happens to its kinetic energy?

options.why_wrong: wrongly assumes kinetic energy scales the same way the speed does, ignoring that speed is squared in the formula.
ignores that the speed, and therefore the kinetic energy, has changed at all.

options.text: It increases by a factor of 8.
options.why_wrong: overstates the scaling; the correct factor is the square of 2, which is 4, not 8.

mcq.explanation: $E_k=\tfrac12\times1.0\times2.0^2=2.0\,\mathrm{J}$ and $E_k=\tfrac12\times1.0\times4.0^2=8.0\,\mathrm{J}$: a factor of 4, because the speed is squared.

mcq.stem: A $2.0\,\mathrm{kg}$ object is raised $10.0\,\mathrm{m}$ vertically. What is its change in gravitational potential energy?

options.why_wrong: calculates only $m\times\Delta h$, leaving out the gravitational field strength $g$ entirely.
wrongly borrows the kinetic-energy formula's structure, calculating $\tfrac12\times2.0\times10.0^2$ instead of $mg\Delta h$.
calculates only $m\times g$ (the object's weight), leaving out the height entirely.

mcq.explanation: $\Delta E_p=2.0\times9.8\times10.0=196\,\mathrm{J}$.

mcq.stem: A $0.10\,\mathrm{kg}$ ball moves at $20\,\mathrm{m/s}$. What is its kinetic energy?

options.why_wrong: leaves out the factor of one-half.
forgets to square the speed, calculating $\tfrac12\times0.10\times20$ instead.
wrongly uses the gravitational potential energy formula, calculating $mg v$ instead of $\tfrac12 mv^2$.

mcq.explanation: $E_k=\tfrac12\times0.10\times20^2=\tfrac12\times0.10\times400=20\,\mathrm{J}$.

flashcards.front: Write the kinetic energy equation, with units.
flashcards.back: $E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$, with $m$ in kg, $v$ in m/s and $E_k$ in J.

flashcards.front: Write the gravitational potential energy equation, with units.
flashcards.back: $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$, with $m$ in kg, $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, $\Delta h$ in m, and $\Delta E_p$ in J.

flashcards.front: If an object's speed doubles, does its kinetic energy double too?
flashcards.back: No. Because $v$ is squared in $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$, doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

flashcards.front: How does kinetic energy's dependence on speed differ from gravitational potential energy's dependence on height?
flashcards.back: Kinetic energy depends on the square of the speed ($v^2$), so doubling speed quadruples $E_k$. Gravitational potential energy depends directly on height ($\Delta h$), so doubling the height simply doubles $\Delta E_p$.

flashcards.front: An object is dragged up a slope. Which distance goes into ΔEp = mgΔh: the slope length or the vertical height gained?
flashcards.back: Only the vertical height gained, Δh, measured straight up; the length of the slope itself is never used in this formula.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Doubling an object's speed only doubles its kinetic energy.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Most other quantities in this unit scale directly (doubling force or doubling distance doubles work), so it is natural to expect speed to behave the same way.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner multiplies the original kinetic energy by the same factor the speed was scaled by, instead of by that factor squared.
misconceptions.correct_model: Because $v$ is squared in $E_k=\tfrac12 mv^2$, doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy (doubling squared is $2^2=4$); tripling the speed multiplies it by nine.
misconceptions.remediation: Calculate both kinetic energies explicitly from the formula, side by side, and compare the ratio of the results rather than guessing the scaling.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The height to use in $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$ is the total distance travelled, including along a slope.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: A question often states a single distance travelled, such as the length of a ramp or hill, and it is tempting to use whichever distance is given.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner uses the length of a slope or path in the formula instead of the vertical height actually gained.
misconceptions.correct_model: $\Delta h$ in the gravitational potential energy equation is always the vertical height gained, measured straight up, never the length of a sloped or curved path travelled to reach it.
misconceptions.remediation: Sketch the vertical height as a separate, clearly marked line next to any slope or path before substituting a value into the formula.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The gravitational field strength $g$ is used with units of newtons rather than N/kg.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The number 9.8 appears in several formulas connected to weight and force, and learners often copy a unit from a neighbouring calculation without checking it.
misconceptions.correct_model: $g$ is a field strength, measured in N/kg (equivalent to m/s²): it tells you how many newtons of weight each kilogram of mass experiences. It is never itself a force in newtons.
misconceptions.remediation: Write out the unit of every quantity substituted into $mg\Delta h$ before multiplying, and check that kg × N/kg × m gives N·m = J.
related_exercises: every gravitational potential energy calculation in this lesson

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming kinetic energy scales directly with speed, so doubling speed is thought to double $E_k$.
common_mistakes.why: Most other quantities in this unit scale directly, so it feels natural for speed to behave the same way.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate both kinetic energies from the formula and compare the ratio directly, rather than assuming a simple scaling.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using the length of a slope or path instead of the vertical height gained in ΔEp = mgΔh.
common_mistakes.why: A question often states only one distance, which looks like 'the' distance to use.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Sketch the vertical height as its own separate line before substituting into the formula; only that vertical line counts.

common_mistakes.mistake: Writing $g$'s unit as newtons (N) instead of N/kg.
common_mistakes.why: The number 9.8 appears in several force-related calculations, so its unit is easy to copy incorrectly.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Write the unit of every quantity before multiplying, and check kg × N/kg × m gives joules.

exam_notes: Always square the speed before applying the other factors in $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$; write $v^2$ as its own step to avoid order-of-operations slips.
When a question gives both a slope length and a vertical height (or lets you work one out), use only the vertical height in $\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$.
State $g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$ explicitly in your working; an omitted or wrongly-labelled $g$ loses marks even if the final number is close.

summary.big_idea: Kinetic energy depends on the square of an object's speed, while gravitational potential energy depends directly on the vertical height it has gained, and these two different dependences must not be confused with each other.
key_points: $E_k=\tfrac12mv^2$: doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy, because $v$ is squared.
$\Delta E_p=mg\Delta h$: only the vertical height gained counts, never the length of a slope or path.
$g=9.8\,\mathrm{N/kg}$, not newtons; always check units before multiplying.

Falling or swinging objects exchange kinetic and gravitational potential energy. If air resistance, friction and other energy transfers are negligible, the total kinetic plus gravitational potential energy remains constant.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Square the speed in the kinetic energy formula; use only the vertical height, never the slope length, in the gravitational potential energy formula.

objectives.statement: Calculate power using $P=W/t=\Delta E/t$, given energy transferred (or work done) and the time taken.

prerequisites.statement: Recall that work done equals energy transferred, $W=Fd=\Delta E$, from the previous lesson.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Power divides exactly this same energy-transferred quantity by the time it took, so it reuses $W$ (or $\Delta E$) directly rather than introducing a new kind of energy.

prerequisites.statement: Convert a percentage to a decimal and back (for example, $40\%=0.40$), and calculate one quantity as a percentage of another.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Efficiency is reported as a percentage, so confident percentage arithmetic is needed before the physics can be trusted.

prerequisites.statement: State that energy is measured in joules and time in seconds.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The power formula divides a joule value by a second value, so both units need to already be clear before the result (in watts) can be interpreted.

theory_blocks.title: Same energy, different time: which device is more powerful?
theory_blocks.body:
Two kettles each transfer exactly 1000 J of electrical energy to heat water. One takes 100 s to do it; the other, a more powerful kettle, takes only 50 s.

Both transfer the same total energy, so 'energy transferred' alone cannot tell them apart. What's different is the **rate** at which each kettle transfers that energy: the faster kettle delivers the same 1000 J twice as quickly.

This rate, energy transferred per second, is called [[blue:**power**]], and it is the idea this lesson formalises first, before turning to a separate question: how much of that transferred energy actually ends up useful.

theory_blocks.title: Power: P = W/t = ΔE/t
theory_blocks.body:
Power is the rate of energy transfer:

$$P=\frac{W}{t}=\frac{\Delta E}{t}$$

with work done or energy transferred ($W$ or $\Delta E$) in joules, time $t$ in seconds, and power $P$ in **watts (W)**, where $1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}$.

The watt is a genuinely different unit from the joule: it describes a rate, not an amount, exactly as speed (m/s) describes a rate of distance covered rather than an amount of distance.

Rearranged, $W=Pt$ lets you find the total energy transferred once you know a device's power and how long it runs for.

theory_blocks.title: More powerful does not mean more efficient
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to treat 'powerful' and 'efficient' as the same kind of compliment, but they answer different questions. Power asks: how fast does this device transfer energy?

Efficiency, introduced next, asks: what fraction of that transferred energy is actually useful? [[blue:A very powerful device can waste most of its input just as easily as a weak one]], and [[orange:a slow, low-power device can be excellent at avoiding waste]].

The two ratings are independent, and a real device needs both measured separately before you can judge it fully.

theory_blocks.title: Efficiency: what fraction of the input is useful?
theory_blocks.body:
As the energy-flow diagrams from earlier lessons showed, a device's input energy always splits between a useful output and energy that spreads elsewhere, typically into internal (thermal) energy of the surroundings.

**Efficiency** is the fraction of the total input that ends up as the useful output.

No real device reaches 100% efficiency: some input always spreads to a not-useful store, however well designed the device is. An efficiency close to 100% describes a device that wastes very little;

an efficiency of, say, 30% describes one where most of the input energy does not end up doing its intended job.

theory_blocks.title: Calculating efficiency as a percentage
theory_blocks.body:
Efficiency is calculated as

$$\text{efficiency}=\frac{\text{useful output (energy or power)}}{\text{total input (energy or power)}}\times100\%$$

using either energies on both sides of the ratio, or powers on both sides, but never a mixture of the two.

In the figure below, a device with 100 J of input energy delivers 65 J usefully, with 35 J spreading elsewhere: efficiency $=\dfrac{65}{100}\times100\%=65\%$.

Checking: $65\,\mathrm{J}+35\,\mathrm{J}=100\,\mathrm{J}$, so nothing has been left out of the diagram.

assets.caption: A device with 100 J of input delivers 65 J usefully and spreads 35 J elsewhere: efficiency = 65/100 × 100% = 65%, and 65 J + 35 J = 100 J checks the diagram is complete.
assets.purpose: Make the input/useful/wasted split and the resulting efficiency percentage visually checkable with verified numbers, without using a Sankey diagram.

theory_blocks.title: Why efficiency can never exceed 100%
theory_blocks.body:
If a calculated efficiency comes out above 100%, something has gone wrong, never a genuinely excellent device.

[[red:An efficiency above 100% would mean more useful energy leaves a device than total energy entered it]]: extra energy would have to appear from nowhere, which breaks conservation of energy.

The most common cause of this error is dividing the wrong way round, useful energy as the denominator instead of the numerator, so checking that the useful amount is on top is always worth a second look.

keywords.definition: Work done per unit time, or energy transferred per unit time: $P=W/t=\Delta E/t$, measured in watts.
The SI unit of power; $1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}$.
The fraction, usually expressed as a percentage, of the total input energy or power that is usefully transferred.
The part of a device's output that serves its intended purpose.
Energy transferred to a store other than the intended useful one, typically internal (thermal) energy of the surroundings.

worked_examples.statement: **A simple power calculation.** A motor transfers $600\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy in $20\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate its power.
reasoning: Apply $P=W/t$.
Divide the energy by the time.
worked_examples.solution: $P=600\,\mathrm{J}\div20\,\mathrm{s}=30\,\mathrm{W}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: This means the motor transfers, on average, 30 J of energy every second.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Multiplying 600 by 20 instead of dividing, giving an answer far too large.

worked_examples.statement: **A first efficiency calculation.** A device receives $500\,\mathrm{J}$ of input energy and usefully transfers $150\,\mathrm{J}$ of it. Calculate its efficiency.
reasoning: Apply efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{useful}}{\text{total}}\times100\%$.
Divide the useful output by the total input, then multiply by 100.
worked_examples.solution: Efficiency $=\dfrac{150}{500}\times100\%=30\%$.
worked_examples.interpretation: 70% of the input energy, $350\,\mathrm{J}$, spreads elsewhere, most likely into internal (thermal) energy.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Dividing 500 by 150 instead of 150 by 500, which would give a result above 100%.

worked_examples.statement: **Power versus efficiency.** Device A has a power of $500\,\mathrm{W}$, and 60% of the energy it transfers each second is useful. Device B has a power of only $300\,\mathrm{W}$, but 90% of the energy it transfers each second is useful. Calculate the useful power delivered by each device, and state which device is more efficient and which is more powerful.
unknowns: which is more powerful; which is more efficient
reasoning: Multiply each device's total power by its useful fraction to find its useful power.
Compare the two devices' total power separately from their efficiency.
worked_examples.solution: Device A's useful power $=500\,\mathrm{W}\times0.60=300\,\mathrm{W}$. Device B's useful power $=300\,\mathrm{W}\times0.90=270\,\mathrm{W}$. Device A is more powerful (500 W vs 300 W), but device B is more efficient (90% vs 60%).
worked_examples.interpretation: Despite being less powerful, device B's useful power (270 W) is close to device A's (300 W), because its much higher efficiency largely makes up for its lower total power.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming the device with the higher power rating must automatically be the better, more efficient choice.

worked_examples.statement: **Power and efficiency together.** A motor has a power of $2000\,\mathrm{W}$ and runs for $5\,\mathrm{s}$, usefully transferring $8000\,\mathrm{J}$ to a load. (a) Calculate the total energy the motor transfers in this time. (b) Calculate the motor's efficiency.
reasoning: Use $W=Pt$ to find the total energy from the power and the time.
Divide the useful output by this total, then multiply by 100, for the efficiency.
worked_examples.solution: (a) $W=2000\,\mathrm{W}\times5\,\mathrm{s}=10\,000\,\mathrm{J}$. (b) Efficiency $=\dfrac{8000}{10\,000}\times100\%=80\%$.
worked_examples.interpretation: This question needs both equations in sequence: power and time give the total energy first, and only then can the useful fraction be compared against it.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Using the power (2000 W) directly as if it were the total energy, instead of first multiplying by the time.

guided_exercises.statement: A pump transfers $900\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy in $30\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate its power.
hints: Write down $P=W/t$ before substituting.
Divide the energy by the time.
State your answer in watts.
common_errors: Giving the answer as '30 J' instead of '30 W'.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Write down $P=W/t$ before substituting.

**Step 2 — Method:** Divide the energy by the time.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** $P=900\,\mathrm{J}\div30\,\mathrm{s}=30\,\mathrm{W}$.

**Step 4 — Check:** State your answer in watts.

guided_exercises.statement: A device receives $200\,\mathrm{J}$ of input energy and usefully transfers $60\,\mathrm{J}$. Calculate its efficiency.
hints: Write down efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{useful}}{\text{total}}\times100\%$.
Make sure the useful amount (the smaller number) is on top.
Multiply your decimal result by 100 to express it as a percentage.
common_errors: Calculating $60/200=0.3$ and forgetting to multiply by 100, giving '0.3%' instead of '30%'.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Write down efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{useful}}{\text{total}}\times100\%$.

**Step 2 — Method:** Make sure the useful amount (the smaller number) is on top.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** Efficiency $=\dfrac{60}{200}\times100\%=30\%$.

**Step 4 — Check:** Multiply your decimal result by 100 to express it as a percentage.

exercises.statement: A crane transfers $1500\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy in $25\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate its power.
exercises.answer: $P=1500\,\mathrm{J}\div25\,\mathrm{s}=60\,\mathrm{W}$.

exercises.statement: A solar panel receives $250\,\mathrm{J}$ of light energy and usefully converts $100\,\mathrm{J}$ of it into electrical energy. Calculate its efficiency.
exercises.answer: Efficiency $=\dfrac{100}{250}\times100\%=40\%$.

exercises.statement: A heater has a power of $800\,\mathrm{W}$ and runs for $15\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the total energy it transfers in this time.
exercises.answer: $W=Pt=800\,\mathrm{W}\times15\,\mathrm{s}=12\,000\,\mathrm{J}$ (12 kJ).
exercises.full_solution: This uses the rearranged power equation, $W=Pt$, rather than dividing.

exercises.statement: A filament lamp has an input power of $60\,\mathrm{W}$ and a useful light-output power of only $9\,\mathrm{W}$. Calculate its efficiency, and explain, using the idea of energy stores from earlier in this unit, what happens to the rest of the input power.
exercises.answer: Efficiency $=\dfrac{9}{60}\times100\%=15\%$. The remaining $51\,\mathrm{W}$ ($60-9$) spreads mainly into the internal (thermal) energy of the lamp's filament, glass and surrounding air, which is why a lit filament lamp feels warm.
exercises.full_solution: Efficiency $=\dfrac{9}{60}\times100\%=15\%$. The remaining $51\,\mathrm{W}$ ($60-9$) spreads mainly into the internal (thermal) energy of the lamp's filament, glass and surrounding air, which is why a lit filament lamp feels warm.

exam_questions.statement: A water pump transfers $5000\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy input, producing $3000\,\mathrm{J}$ of useful output. (a) Calculate the pump's efficiency. (b) If this energy transfer takes $25\,\mathrm{s}$, calculate the pump's input power.
mark_scheme: States efficiency as $60\%$.
Applies $P=W/t$ with $W=5000\,\mathrm{J}$ and $t=25\,\mathrm{s}$.
States power as $200\,\mathrm{W}$, with correct unit.
common_errors: Using the useful energy (3000 J) instead of the total input (5000 J) when calculating the power in part (b).

exam_questions.statement: A motor has an input power of $150\,\mathrm{W}$ and runs for $40\,\mathrm{s}$. Its efficiency is $80\%$. Calculate (a) the total energy input to the motor, and (b) the useful energy output.
mark_scheme: Applies $W=Pt$ with $P=150\,\mathrm{W}$ and $t=40\,\mathrm{s}$.
States total energy as $6000\,\mathrm{J}$.
Converts $80\%$ to the decimal $0.80$ and multiplies by $6000\,\mathrm{J}$.
States useful energy as $4800\,\mathrm{J}$.
common_errors: Treating the 80% as the wasted fraction instead of the useful fraction, and calculating $6000\times0.20=1200\,\mathrm{J}$ by mistake.

challenge_questions.statement: Extended: Explain how the principles covered in "Power and efficiency" apply to a real-world situation. Include relevant equations and units in your answer.
challenge_questions.answer: A complete answer links the physics concepts from power and efficiency to practical scenarios, using correct equations, SI units, and scientific reasoning.
challenge_questions.full_solution:
Step 1: State the relevant physics principles from Power and efficiency.
Step 2: Identify a real-world application.
Step 3: Apply the equations with correct units.
Step 4: Evaluate your answer for physical reasonableness.

mcq.stem: A device transfers $400\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy in $8\,\mathrm{s}$. What is its power?

options.why_wrong: multiplies the energy by the time instead of dividing.
divides the time by the energy instead of the energy by the time.
has the correct number but the wrong unit; power is measured in watts, not joules.

mcq.explanation: $P=400\,\mathrm{J}\div8\,\mathrm{s}=50\,\mathrm{W}$.

mcq.stem: A machine receives $50\,\mathrm{J}$ of input energy and usefully transfers $25\,\mathrm{J}$. What is its efficiency?

options.why_wrong: divides the total by the useful amount instead of the useful amount by the total, giving an impossible result above 100%.
wrongly treats the useful output as if it were also the total input.
correctly divides 25 by 50 but forgets to multiply the result by 100.

mcq.explanation: Efficiency $=\dfrac{25}{50}\times100\%=50\%$.

mcq.stem: A kettle transfers $3000\,\mathrm{J}$ of energy in 1 minute. What is its power, in watts?

options.why_wrong: forgets to convert 1 minute into 60 seconds, effectively dividing by 1 second instead.
adds the energy and the time together instead of dividing one by the other.
divides the time by the energy instead of the energy by the time.

mcq.explanation: 1 minute $=60\,\mathrm{s}$, so $P=3000\,\mathrm{J}\div60\,\mathrm{s}=50\,\mathrm{W}$.

mcq.stem: A device receives $80\,\mathrm{J}$ of input energy and wastes $60\,\mathrm{J}$, which spreads into the internal (thermal) store of the surroundings. What is its efficiency?

options.why_wrong: reports the wasted fraction ($60/80$) instead of the useful fraction.
divides the useful energy by the wasted energy ($20/60$) instead of by the total input.
uses the wasted energy value directly as if it were already a percentage, without calculating a ratio at all.

mcq.explanation: Useful output $=80-60=20\,\mathrm{J}$, so efficiency $=\dfrac{20}{80}\times100\%=25\%$.

flashcards.front: Write the power equation and its unit.
flashcards.back: $P=W/t=\Delta E/t$, measured in watts (W), where $1\,\mathrm{W}=1\,\mathrm{J/s}$.

flashcards.front: Write the equation for efficiency as a percentage.
flashcards.back: Efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{useful output}}{\text{total input}}\times100\%$, using either energies or powers on both sides, never a mixture.

flashcards.front: Can a real device's efficiency be above 100%?
flashcards.back: No. That would mean more useful energy leaves the device than total energy entered it, creating energy from nothing, which breaks conservation of energy.

flashcards.front: How do power and efficiency differ, even though both sound like measures of how 'good' a device is?
flashcards.back: Power measures how fast a device transfers energy (J/s). Efficiency measures what fraction of that transferred energy is usefully used. A device can be powerful yet inefficient, or the reverse.

flashcards.front: Two devices transfer the same total energy, but device A takes half the time device B takes. Which has the greater power?
flashcards.back: Device A. Transferring the same energy in less time means a greater rate of transfer, which is exactly what power measures.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Power and energy are interchangeable, so a 'more powerful' device simply has 'more energy'.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both words are used loosely in everyday speech to mean roughly 'how much a device can do'.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner compares two devices' energy transferred without reference to time, while discussing which is 'more powerful'.
misconceptions.correct_model: Power is the rate of energy transfer (joules per second), not an amount of energy on its own. The same energy transferred in less time means greater power, even though the total energy transferred has not changed.
misconceptions.remediation: Always ask 'how much energy, and over what time?' before comparing two devices' power, and calculate P=W/t explicitly rather than comparing energy totals alone.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A device's efficiency can be above 100% if it is good enough, without any extra energy input.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Dividing the wrong way round (total ÷ useful instead of useful ÷ total) produces a number above 100%, which can look like a plausible 'very good' result if the meaning is not checked.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner reports an efficiency greater than 100% without flagging it as impossible.
misconceptions.correct_model: Efficiency can never exceed 100%, because that would mean more useful energy leaves the device than the total energy that entered it, creating energy from nothing and breaking conservation of energy. Every source of energy a device uses counts as part of its total input.
misconceptions.remediation: Check which number is divided by which: the useful amount must always be the smaller (or equal) number on top, giving a result of 100% or less.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An efficiency calculation can divide an output given in watts by an input given in joules, or vice versa, without converting.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both units appear together throughout this lesson, which makes it easy to divide values that are not actually of the same kind.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner substitutes a power value (W) and an energy value (J) directly into the same efficiency ratio.
misconceptions.correct_model: Both quantities in an efficiency ratio must be the same kind: either both energies, in joules, or both powers, in watts. Mixing the two without converting gives a meaningless number.
misconceptions.remediation: Before dividing, write down the unit of each quantity in the ratio and check they match; convert one if they do not.
related_exercises: every efficiency calculation in this lesson

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a 'more powerful' device as automatically 'more efficient'.
common_mistakes.why: Both words sound like general measures of how good a device is.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Calculate power and efficiency separately: power compares energy transferred per second, efficiency compares useful output to total input, and the two do not have to agree.

common_mistakes.why: Dividing the wrong way round (total ÷ useful instead of useful ÷ total) produces a result above 100%.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check that the useful amount, which is always the smaller or equal number, is on top of the fraction; a result over 100% means you have divided the wrong way.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dividing a power in watts by an energy in joules (or the reverse) when calculating efficiency.
common_mistakes.why: Both units appear throughout this lesson, making it easy to combine values that are not actually comparable.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check that both quantities in the efficiency ratio are the same kind, either both energies or both powers, before dividing.

exam_notes: Convert any time given in minutes (or other non-second units) into seconds before applying $P=W/t$.
An efficiency calculation always places the useful amount over the total amount; an answer above 100% means the division has very likely been done the wrong way round.
State clearly whether an efficiency is being calculated from energies (J) or from powers (W), and never mix the two in a single ratio.

summary.big_idea: Power measures how fast energy is transferred, while efficiency measures what fraction of that transfer is useful, and a device can rate highly on one without rating highly on the other.
key_points: P = W/t = ΔE/t, measured in watts, where 1 W = 1 J/s.
Efficiency = (useful output ÷ total input) × 100%, using matching units on both sides.
No real device can have an efficiency above 100%, since that would require creating energy from nothing.
A more powerful device transfers energy faster, but is not automatically more efficient.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Keep power (how fast) and efficiency (how useful) as two separate questions about a device, each answered by its own ratio.

objectives.statement: Describe the generation route to electricity for fossil, biofuel, water (hydroelectric), geothermal, nuclear, solar and wind resources, and compare resources using stated criteria rather than a single absolute ranking.
Identify which energy resources have a solar origin and which are the stated exceptions (geothermal, nuclear, tidal), and distinguish nuclear fusion in the Sun from nuclear fission in a reactor.

prerequisites.statement: Recall the four transfer pathways from earlier in this unit: mechanical work, electrical work, heating and waves.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Every resource's generation route in this lesson is described using exactly these same pathways, so recognising them lets a new route be understood within a familiar framework rather than learned from nothing.

prerequisites.statement: Recall that power is the rate of energy transfer and that efficiency compares useful output with total input, from the previous lesson.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Comparing resources by 'scale' or 'reliability' often means comparing the power and efficiency of their generation routes, so these ideas are reused directly rather than reintroduced.

theory_blocks.title: Behind every socket, a specific chain of transfers
theory_blocks.body:
Electricity from a wall socket looks identical no matter where it came from, but it is never the end of the story: trace it backwards and you always find [[blue:a specific chain of energy stores and transfer pathways]], starting from some original source.

A coal power station's chain starts in the chemical store of ancient buried plant matter; a solar panel's chain starts in light arriving from the Sun.

Both chains end in the same place, electrical energy, but they could hardly look more different further back.

This lesson is about learning to trace that chain for each major resource, and then using what you find to compare resources sensibly, rather than treating 'best energy source' as if it had one single, universal answer.

theory_blocks.title: Three kinds of generation route
theory_blocks.body:
Almost every electricity-generating resource falls into one of three patterns:

1. **Needs a boiler.** A fuel is burned, or a heat source is used, to boil water into high-pressure steam, which turns a turbine connected to a generator. Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas), biofuels, nuclear fission and some geothermal plants all work this way; only the heat source differs between them.
2. **Turns a turbine directly, no boiler.** Moving water (hydroelectric dams, waves and tides) or moving air (wind) pushes directly on a turbine's blades, turning the turbine, with no fuel burned and no steam produced at all.
3. **No turbine at all.** Solar cells (photovoltaic panels) convert light directly into electrical energy, with no turbine, no generator spun by a fluid, and no boiler anywhere in the process.

The figure below sets all three patterns side by side. One useful resource does not fit any of them, because it never produces electricity: a solar thermal collector simply heats water, and it is described in the next block.

assets.caption: Three generation-route patterns compared: a boiler-and-steam route (top), a direct-turbine route using moving water or air (middle), and a no-turbine route using solar cells (bottom).
assets.purpose: Make explicit that a boiler is only one of three route patterns, directly targeting the misconception that every generation route needs one.

theory_blocks.title: Water routes, and the two ways of using the Sun
theory_blocks.body:
**Water: dams, waves and tides.** Three different water resources all finish in the same way, with moving water pushing directly on a turbine that drives a generator.

- A **hydroelectric dam** holds water in a reservoir above the turbine hall. The water is released through pipes and its weight makes it fall, so it arrives moving fast and pushes on the turbine's blades.
- A **wave generator** floats at sea, where passing waves make a float, or a column of water trapped inside a chamber, rise and fall. That repeated up-and-down movement is used to turn a turbine or drive a generator.
- A **tidal barrage** is a dam built across the mouth of an estuary. The rising tide fills the estuary through open gates; the gates are then closed, and as the tide falls outside, the trapped water is let out through turbines built into the barrage.

None of the three burns a fuel or boils water, so all three belong to the [[blue:direct-turbine pattern]].

**The Sun: two quite different uses.** A [[blue:solar cell]] (photovoltaic panel) absorbs light from the Sun and produces electricity directly. A [[orange:solar thermal collector]] is not a solar cell at all: dark panels, usually on a roof, absorb infrared and other electromagnetic waves from the Sun and transfer that energy by heating to water flowing through pipes inside them. Its useful output is hot water for the building, not electricity — there is no turbine and no generator anywhere in it. Both make use of radiation from the Sun; only one of them generates electricity.

assets.caption: Waves, tides and falling water all turn a turbine directly; sunlight in a solar cell gives electricity with no turbine; infrared absorbed by a solar thermal collector gives hot water and no electricity at all.
assets.purpose: Set the three water routes beside the two solar routes, so that the solar thermal collector's output (hot water, not electricity) is unmistakable.

theory_blocks.title: Comparing resources needs stated criteria, not one ranking
theory_blocks.body:
Asking 'which energy resource is best?' on its own has no single answer. A fair comparison states which criteria matter for the situation, which commonly include:

- **Availability** — can the resource be used whenever it is needed, or only sometimes (for example, only when it is sunny or windy)?
- **Reliability** — how predictable is the supply from one day, or one season, to the next?
- **Scale** — how much power can a single installation realistically provide, and how many would be needed?
- **Renewability** — is the resource naturally replenished on a human timescale, or will it eventually run out?
- **Environmental impact** — what effect does building, running and (where relevant) fuelling the resource have on land, ecosystems, air and water?

Two different situations can reasonably choose two different resources, each correct for its own stated criteria.

theory_blocks.title: The criteria applied, resource by resource
theory_blocks.body:
The five criteria can now be applied to every resource in turn. Read a row across for the advantages and disadvantages of one resource; read a column down to compare all the resources on one criterion.

| Resource | Renewable? | Available when needed? | Scale | Main environmental impact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) | No | Yes, on demand | Very large | Carbon dioxide released, adding to climate change; sulfur dioxide causing acid rain; damage from mining and drilling |
| Biofuels | Yes, the crop regrows | Yes, once harvested and stored | Small to medium | Carbon dioxide released on burning, partly balanced by the growing crop; land used that could grow food |
| Hydroelectric dams | Yes, the water cycle refills the reservoir | Yes, water can be released at any moment, as long as rainfall keeps the reservoir full | Large | Valleys flooded; river ecosystems and nearby communities disrupted |
| Tides | Yes | Only around the tides, but their times are known years in advance | Medium to large, and only at suitable estuaries | Estuary habitat changed, affecting fish and wading birds |
| Waves | Yes | No, the sea state depends on the weather | Small for each generator | Small; some effect on coastal habitats and on shipping |
| Geothermal | Yes | Yes, day and night, all year round | Medium to large, but only where hot rock is near the surface | Small; drilling, and gases released from underground |
| Nuclear fission | No, uranium is a finite fuel | Yes, on demand | Very large | Radioactive waste that must be stored safely for a very long time, and the risk of release in an accident; no carbon dioxide while running |
| Solar cells | Yes | No, nothing at night and less when cloudy | Small for one panel, large for a solar farm | Very small while running; land and manufacturing materials for large farms |
| Solar thermal collectors | Yes | No, only while the Sun shines, though the hot water can be stored in a tank | One building, and it supplies hot water rather than electricity | Very small |
| Wind | Yes | No, only when the wind blows, and turbines shut down in a storm | Medium, so many turbines are needed | Land or seabed used; noise and visual impact; a hazard to birds |

Notice that no row is good on everything. Fossil fuels and nuclear fission win on availability and scale but lose on renewability and waste; wind, waves and solar cells win on renewability but lose on reliability;

tides are renewable and predictable but only work at certain places and certain times.

In an exam, always say [[blue:which criterion]] your point belongs to. 'Wind is renewable, but it is unreliable because it generates nothing when the wind drops' earns the marks; 'wind is good for the environment' does not.

theory_blocks.title: Most resources trace back to the Sun
theory_blocks.body:
Several resources that look unrelated to sunlight are, on tracing their chain back far enough, solar in origin:

- **Wind** — the Sun heats different parts of the Earth's surface and atmosphere unevenly; these temperature differences drive air movement, which we experience and harness as wind.
- **Water (hydroelectric)** — the Sun's heat evaporates water from oceans and lakes, which later falls as rain and collects in rivers and reservoirs, ready to turn a turbine.
- **Biofuels** — plants store chemical energy through photosynthesis, which is powered by sunlight; this stored chemical energy is later released by burning.

Fossil fuels are also ultimately solar in origin, since they formed from ancient plant and marine matter that once captured sunlight through photosynthesis, though on a timescale far too slow to count as renewable.

theory_blocks.title: Three exceptions: geothermal, nuclear and tidal
theory_blocks.body:
Three resources are explicit exceptions to the solar-origin pattern:

- [[blue:**Geothermal**]] energy comes from heat generated deep inside the Earth, largely from the slow radioactive decay of elements in the Earth's crust and mantle, not from sunlight reaching the surface.
- [[orange:**Nuclear**]] energy comes from the nuclei of atoms (uranium, in current reactors), released by nuclear fission, which has nothing to do with sunlight at all.
- [[teal:**Tidal**]] energy comes mainly from the gravitational pull of the Moon (and, to a lesser extent, the Sun) on the oceans, combined with the Earth's rotation, not from solar heating.

These three exceptions are worth learning as a short, fixed list, since every other resource in this lesson does trace back to the Sun.

theory_blocks.title: Fission in a reactor, fusion in the Sun
theory_blocks.body:
Nuclear [[blue:**fission**]] splits a large, unstable nucleus (such as uranium-235) into smaller nuclei, releasing energy; this is the reaction used in every nuclear power station currently operating on Earth.

Nuclear [[orange:**fusion**]] joins small nuclei (such as hydrogen) together into a larger nucleus, also releasing energy; this is the reaction that powers the Sun and other stars.

The two reactions are opposite in direction (splitting versus joining) and are not interchangeable: no power station on Earth currently generates electricity from fusion.

The detailed nuclear mechanisms behind either reaction are outside this unit; what matters here is keeping the two processes, and where each occurs, clearly separate.

keywords.definition: The chain of energy stores and transfer pathways from a resource's original energy store to the electricity it produces.
A resource that is replenished naturally on a timescale short enough to be used repeatedly, unlike a finite resource such as a fossil fuel.
A machine turned by a moving fluid (steam, water or air) that drives a generator to produce electricity.
A nuclear reaction in which a large nucleus splits into smaller nuclei, releasing energy; used in nuclear power stations.
A nuclear reaction in which small nuclei join together, releasing energy; the process that powers the Sun.
A panel that absorbs infrared and other electromagnetic waves from the Sun and transfers the energy by heating to water flowing through it; its useful output is hot water, not electricity.

worked_examples.statement: **A hydroelectric dam's route.** State whether a hydroelectric dam uses a boiler to generate electricity, and describe how it actually turns its turbine.
reasoning: Identify which of the three route patterns (boiler, direct turbine, no turbine) this resource matches.
Hydroelectric power uses moving water directly, so it falls into the direct-turbine pattern.
worked_examples.solution: No boiler is used. The moving or falling water itself pushes directly on the turbine's blades, turning the turbine, which is connected to a generator that produces the electricity. No fuel is burned and no steam is produced anywhere in the process.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is the clearest example of the direct-turbine pattern, and a useful one to contrast against any fuel-burning route.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing the dam as 'boiling the water' to make steam, confusing it with the fossil-fuel route.

worked_examples.statement: **Geothermal versus coal.** A geothermal power station and a coal power station both ultimately turn a steam turbine. State one way their routes are similar, and one way they differ.
reasoning: Both routes end the same way: steam turning a turbine connected to a generator, so look there first for the similarity.
Compare where the heat that produces the steam actually comes from, for the difference.
worked_examples.solution:
Similarity: both use heat to boil water into steam, which turns a turbine connected to a generator.

Difference: the coal station burns a fuel (releasing its stored chemical energy) to produce that heat, while the geothermal station uses naturally occurring heat from deep underground, with no fuel burned at all.
worked_examples.interpretation: This is a useful pattern for comparing any two 'boiler' routes: the turbine-and-generator stage is always the same, so the real difference is always in how the heat is produced.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Describing geothermal energy as if it also burned a fuel, instead of identifying that its heat is already present underground.

worked_examples.statement: **Choosing for a specific situation.** An isolated weather station on a very windy hillside needs a continuous, reliable electricity supply through the night as well as the day, but has no connection to a national electricity grid. Explain why neither wind power alone nor a diesel generator alone is an obviously 'best' choice, using named criteria.
knowns: resource options: wind power; diesel generator
requirement: continuous, reliable supply, including overnight, off-grid
unknowns: which criteria make each option incomplete on its own
reasoning: Check wind power against reliability: wind is not guaranteed to blow continuously, even on a windy hillside, so supply could fail at any time without storage.
Check a diesel generator against renewability and fuel availability: it can run continuously on demand, but needs a regular, delivered fuel supply to an isolated site, and burns a non-renewable fuel.
worked_examples.solution:
Wind power alone fails on reliability: without a calm-weather backup or energy storage (such as batteries), the station could lose power whenever the wind drops, including at night.

A diesel generator alone fails on renewability and long-term fuel logistics: it can supply continuous, reliable power on demand, but depends on a non-renewable fuel that must be regularly delivered to an isolated site.

A combination, such as wind power with battery storage and a small diesel backup, addresses more of the criteria than either resource alone.
worked_examples.interpretation: There is no single 'best' resource here, only a set of trade-offs against stated criteria that a combined system can address better than either resource alone.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Declaring one resource simply 'better' than the other without checking it against every stated requirement of the situation.

worked_examples.statement: **A fossil-fuel route, in full.** Describe the full route by which a fossil-fuel (for example, coal) power station generates electricity, then state one similarity and one difference between this route and a nuclear power station's route.
unknowns: one similarity and one difference with the nuclear route
reasoning: Trace the fossil-fuel route stage by stage: fuel, heat, steam, turbine, generator.
Compare this to the nuclear route at the point where the heat source differs.
worked_examples.interpretation: Describing a full route stage by stage, rather than jumping straight from 'fuel' to 'electricity', is exactly what exam-style route questions expect.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Skipping the steam stage, or describing the turbine as if it were the generator (they are two separate, connected machines).

guided_exercises.statement: State whether a wind turbine uses a boiler, and briefly describe how it generates electricity.
hints: Decide which of the three route patterns (boiler, direct turbine, no turbine) wind power matches.
Describe what physically pushes on the turbine's blades.
State what the turbine is connected to.
guided_exercises.answer: No boiler is used. Moving air pushes directly on the turbine's blades, turning the turbine, which is connected to a generator that converts the kinetic energy of the turning turbine directly into electrical energy.
common_errors: Describing wind power as needing to 'heat up' air first, instead of the air's own motion directly turning the turbine.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Decide which of the three route patterns (boiler, direct turbine, no turbine) wind power matches.

**Step 2 — Method:** Describe what physically pushes on the turbine's blades.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** No boiler is used. Moving air pushes directly on the turbine's blades, turning the turbine, which is connected to a generator that converts the kinetic energy of the turning turbine directly into electrical energy.

**Step 4 — Check:** State what the turbine is connected to.

guided_exercises.statement: Explain why wind energy is usually described as having a 'solar origin', even though no sunlight is directly involved in turning a turbine.
hints: Think about what causes air to move from one place to another in the first place.
Trace that cause back one more step, to the Sun.
guided_exercises.answer: The Sun heats different parts of the Earth's surface and atmosphere unevenly. These uneven temperatures cause air to rise, fall and move from warmer regions to cooler ones, which is what we observe and harness as wind. So although sunlight does not push the turbine directly, the energy driving the wind ultimately traces back to the Sun.
common_errors: Concluding that because sunlight isn't directly involved, wind cannot be solar in origin, without tracing the cause of air movement back far enough.
guided_exercises.full_solution:
**Step 1 — Identify:** Think about what causes air to move from one place to another in the first place.

**Step 2 — Method:** Trace that cause back one more step, to the Sun.

**Step 3 — Calculate:** The Sun heats different parts of the Earth's surface and atmosphere unevenly. These uneven temperatures cause air to rise, fall and move from warmer regions to cooler ones, which is what we observe and harness as wind. So although sunlight does not push the turbine directly, the energy driving the wind ultimately traces back to the Sun.

exercises.statement: Name two renewable energy resources that have a solar origin, and briefly state the chain linking each one back to the Sun.
exercises.answer: Wind: the Sun heats the atmosphere unevenly, driving air movement. Biofuel: plants use photosynthesis, powered by sunlight, to store chemical energy, which is later released by burning. (Water/hydroelectric, via the Sun-driven water cycle, is an equally valid second answer.)
exercises.full_solution: Any two of wind, water (hydroelectric) and biofuel are acceptable, each with its own correctly traced chain back to the Sun.

exercises.statement: Explain why 'renewable' does not mean 'no environmental impact', using one named renewable resource as your example.
exercises.answer: A hydroelectric dam is renewable, because the water cycle continually replenishes the reservoir behind it, but it is not impact-free: building a dam can flood large areas of land, disrupt river ecosystems, and displace wildlife or communities living nearby. Renewability describes replenishment, not the absence of environmental effects.
exercises.full_solution: A wind farm (land use, habitat and visual impact) or a solar farm (land use, manufacturing impact) would be equally valid named examples.

exercises.statement: A nuclear power station and a solar farm are both used to generate electricity on a large scale. State one generation-route difference between them.
exercises.answer: The nuclear station boils water using heat released by nuclear fission in its reactor core, producing steam that turns a turbine connected to a generator; the solar farm's photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electrical energy, with no turbine, no steam and no fuel of any kind.
exercises.full_solution: The nuclear station boils water using heat released by nuclear fission in its reactor core, producing steam that turns a turbine connected to a generator; the solar farm's photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into electrical energy, with no turbine, no steam and no fuel of any kind.

exercises.statement: A tidal barrage is built across the mouth of an estuary. Describe how it generates electricity, and state which of the three generation-route patterns it belongs to.
exercises.answer: The rising tide flows into the estuary through open gates; the gates are then closed to hold the water back. As the tide falls outside the barrage, the trapped water is released through turbines built into the barrage. The moving water pushes directly on the turbine blades, and the turning turbines drive generators. It belongs to the direct-turbine pattern: no fuel is burned and no steam is produced.
exercises.full_solution: The key point is that the water itself does the mechanical work on the turbine, exactly as in a hydroelectric dam or a wave generator; only the reason the water moves (the tide, rather than a reservoir held high up) is different.

exercises.statement: A small coastal town is considering a tidal barrage to generate electricity. Using the idea of solar-origin exceptions from this lesson, explain why tidal energy cannot be described as solar in origin.
exercises.answer: Tidal energy arises mainly from the gravitational pull of the Moon (and, to a lesser extent, the Sun) on the oceans, combined with the Earth's rotation, not from sunlight warming the Earth's surface. Tidal energy is one of the three stated exceptions to the solar-origin pattern, alongside geothermal and nuclear energy.
exercises.full_solution: Tidal energy arises mainly from the gravitational pull of the Moon (and, to a lesser extent, the Sun) on the oceans, combined with the Earth's rotation, not from sunlight warming the Earth's surface. Tidal energy is one of the three stated exceptions to the solar-origin pattern, alongside geothermal and nuclear energy.

exam_questions.statement: Describe the route by which a coal-fired power station generates electricity from the chemical energy stored in coal, naming each energy store and pathway involved in order.
exam_questions.answer: The chemical energy stored in coal is released as heat when the coal is burned. This heat transfers, by heating, to water, turning it into high-pressure steam. The steam does mechanical work on a turbine, making it spin. The spinning turbine turns a generator, which transfers energy electrically to the electricity supply.
exam_questions.full_solution: The chemical energy stored in coal is released as heat when the coal is burned. This heat transfers, by heating, to water, turning it into high-pressure steam. The steam does mechanical work on a turbine, making it spin. The spinning turbine turns a generator, which transfers energy electrically to the electricity supply.
mark_scheme: States that coal's chemical energy is released as heat by burning.
States that this heat turns water into steam (heating pathway).
States that the steam turns the turbine by doing mechanical work.
States that the turbine turns a generator, producing electrical energy.
common_errors: Jumping straight from 'burning coal' to 'electricity', without describing the steam and turbine stages in between.

exam_questions.statement: State two generation routes that do not use a boiler, and for each, name the pathway that drives the turbine (or cell) directly. Then explain, using one named example, why not every energy resource is solar in origin.
exam_questions.answer: Hydroelectric power: moving/falling water does mechanical work directly on the turbine's blades. Wind power: moving air does mechanical work directly on the turbine's blades. (Solar cells are also acceptable: light (a wave) transfers energy directly to the cell, which produces electricity with no turbine at all.) Geothermal energy is not solar in origin: it comes from heat generated deep inside the Earth, largely by the radioactive decay of elements in the Earth's crust and mantle, not from sunlight reaching the surface.
exam_questions.full_solution: Any two of hydroelectric, wind or solar are acceptable for the first part; any one of geothermal, nuclear or tidal, correctly explained, is acceptable for the second part.
mark_scheme: Names a first non-boiler route with its pathway (hydroelectric or wind: mechanical work by moving water/air on the turbine; solar cells: light absorbed directly by the cell).
Names a second, different non-boiler route, again with its pathway stated.
Names one correct non-solar-origin resource (geothermal, nuclear or tidal).
Gives a correct explanation of why that resource is not solar in origin.
common_errors: Naming a boiler-based resource (such as biofuel or nuclear) as a 'non-boiler' route by mistake.

exam_questions.statement:
A country with a long coastline and strong tides is deciding between building a tidal barrage and building a nuclear power station.

(a) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of generating electricity from the tides. [2]

(b) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of generating electricity from nuclear fission. [2]

In each case, name the criterion your point refers to.
exam_questions.answer:
(a) Advantage: tidal energy is renewable, and the times of the tides are known years in advance, so the output is predictable (renewability and reliability). Disadvantage: a barrage generates only around the tides rather than continuously, and it changes the estuary habitat, affecting fish and wading birds (availability and environmental impact).

(b) Advantage: one nuclear station supplies a very large output on demand, and releases no carbon dioxide while it is running (scale, availability and environmental impact). Disadvantage: uranium is a finite fuel, so the resource is non-renewable, and the radioactive waste must be stored safely for a very long time (renewability and environmental impact).
exam_questions.full_solution: Any correct advantage and disadvantage is accepted, provided each is tied to one of the five criteria and is true of that resource: for the tides, the limited number of suitable estuaries is an equally valid disadvantage; for nuclear fission, the risk of release in an accident is an equally valid one.
mark_scheme: Gives one correct advantage of tidal generation, with its criterion named (renewable; predictable, so reliable).
Gives one correct disadvantage of tidal generation, with its criterion named (only generates around the tides; suitable estuaries are rare; estuary habitat damaged).
Gives one correct advantage of nuclear fission, with its criterion named (very large scale; available on demand; no carbon dioxide while running).
Gives one correct disadvantage of nuclear fission, with its criterion named (non-renewable fuel; radioactive waste; accident risk).
common_errors: Giving two points that are really the same criterion twice, such as 'renewable' and 'it will never run out'.
Writing a vague judgement such as 'nuclear is bad for the environment' without saying what the effect actually is.

challenge_questions.answer: A complete answer links the physics concepts from choosing energy resources to practical scenarios, using correct equations, SI units, and scientific reasoning.

mcq.stem: Which of these generation routes does NOT involve a boiler producing steam?

options.why_wrong: coal is burned to boil water into steam, which turns the turbine.
nuclear fission releases heat that boils water into steam, which turns the turbine.
biofuel is burned, just like a fossil fuel, to boil water into steam.

mcq.explanation: A wind turbine is turned directly by moving air; no fuel is burned and no steam is produced.

mcq.stem: Which statement about renewable energy resources is correct?

options.text: Renewable resources have no environmental impact at all.
options.why_wrong: confuses 'replenished naturally' with 'impact-free'; renewable resources such as hydroelectric dams can still have significant environmental effects.

options.text: A resource only counts as renewable if it produces absolutely no waste or disruption.
options.why_wrong: invents a stricter definition than the one actually used; renewability is about replenishment, not impact.

options.text: Fossil fuels are renewable because new fossil fuels are slowly forming underground.
options.why_wrong: fossil fuels do form over millions of years, but far too slowly to be replenished on a human timescale, so they are classified as non-renewable.

options.text: Renewable resources are replenished naturally on a human timescale, but can still have environmental impacts.

mcq.explanation: Renewable describes natural replenishment on a human timescale, not the absence of environmental impact.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes nuclear fission from nuclear fusion?

options.text: Fission splits large nuclei apart and is used in nuclear power stations; fusion joins small nuclei together and powers the Sun.
Fission joins small nuclei together; fusion splits large nuclei apart.
options.why_wrong: swaps the two definitions round.

options.text: Fission and fusion are two names for exactly the same nuclear reaction.
options.why_wrong: ignores that they are different reactions, releasing energy by opposite mechanisms (splitting versus joining).

options.text: Fission occurs only in the Sun, and fusion occurs only in nuclear power stations.
