mcq.stem: Which of these energy resources is NOT considered to have a solar origin?

options.why_wrong: wind has a solar origin: uneven solar heating of the atmosphere drives air movement.
biofuel has a solar origin: photosynthesis, powered by sunlight, stores the chemical energy later released by burning.
hydroelectric power has a solar origin: the Sun drives the water cycle that fills rivers and reservoirs.

mcq.explanation: Geothermal energy comes from heat generated inside the Earth, not from the Sun, making it one of the three stated solar-origin exceptions.

mcq.stem: A flat dark panel on a house roof absorbs radiation from the Sun and heats water flowing through pipes inside it. Which statement about this panel is correct?

options.text: It is a solar cell, so its useful output is electricity.
options.why_wrong: a solar cell converts light directly into electricity; this panel produces no electricity at all.

options.text: It boils the water into steam, which turns a turbine inside the panel.
options.why_wrong: there is no turbine and no generator; the water is heated for direct use, not boiled to drive anything.

options.text: It is a solar thermal collector, so its useful output is hot water.
It is a solar thermal collector, so it supplies the house with both hot water and electricity.
options.why_wrong: a thermal collector has no generator, so it supplies no electricity; separate solar cells would be needed for that.

mcq.explanation: A solar thermal collector absorbs infrared and other electromagnetic waves from the Sun and transfers that energy by heating to the water in its pipes. Hot water is the useful output; only solar cells produce electricity.

flashcards.front: Name three generation routes that need no boiler and burn no fuel.
flashcards.back: Hydroelectric (moving/falling water) and wind (moving air) both turn a turbine directly; solar cells generate electricity directly from light, without any turbine at all.

flashcards.front: What does 'renewable' actually mean, for an energy resource?
flashcards.back: A resource that is replenished naturally on a human timescale, unlike a finite resource such as a fossil fuel. It does not mean the resource has no environmental impact.

flashcards.front: Is every energy resource solar in origin?
flashcards.back: No. Geothermal (Earth's internal heat), nuclear (energy from atomic nuclei) and tidal (gravity of the Moon and Sun, plus Earth's rotation) are the stated exceptions; wind, waves, hydroelectric, biofuels and fossil fuels all trace back to the Sun.

flashcards.front: How do nuclear fission and nuclear fusion differ?
flashcards.back: Fission splits large nuclei apart and is used in nuclear power stations on Earth; fusion joins small nuclei together and is the process that powers the Sun.

flashcards.front: A remote research station needs continuous power through the night. Why might relying on solar power alone be a poor choice, even in a very sunny location?
flashcards.back: Solar cells only generate electricity while sunlight is available, so without additional energy storage (such as batteries) or a complementary supply, a solar-only system cannot reliably supply power overnight.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A renewable resource has no environmental impact at all.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Renewable resources are often praised together as 'green' or 'clean' in everyday discussion, which blurs the distinction between replenishment and impact.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a renewable resource as impact-free, or dismisses any environmental concern about it simply because it is renewable.
misconceptions.correct_model: Renewable means the resource is replenished naturally on a human timescale, not that it is free of environmental impact. A hydroelectric dam, for example, is renewable but can flood land and disrupt river ecosystems; a wind farm is renewable but uses land and materials and affects local habitats.
misconceptions.remediation: Treat renewability and environmental impact as two separate questions about any resource, and answer each one on its own evidence rather than assuming one from the other.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Every method of generating electricity requires a boiler to make steam.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The fossil-fuel, boiler-and-steam-turbine route is the example most commonly pictured first when 'generating electricity' is mentioned.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes a hydroelectric, wind or solar generation route as if it also involved boiling water into steam.
misconceptions.correct_model: A boiler is used only where a fuel or a natural heat source makes steam to turn a turbine (fossil fuel, biofuel, nuclear, and some geothermal plants). Hydroelectric and wind generators turn a turbine directly, using moving water or air, with no boiler at all; solar cells generate electricity directly from light, with no turbine and no boiler at all.
misconceptions.remediation: Before describing a route, ask whether the resource's energy arrives as heat (needing a boiler), as motion (turning a turbine directly), or as light (no turbine at all).

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Nuclear fission and nuclear fusion are the same process.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both involve atomic nuclei and release very large amounts of energy, which makes the two names easy to blur together.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner uses 'fission' and 'fusion' interchangeably, or describes the Sun's energy source as fission.
misconceptions.correct_model: Nuclear fission splits a large nucleus into smaller nuclei, releasing energy; it is the process used in nuclear power stations on Earth. Nuclear fusion joins small nuclei together, releasing energy; it is the process that powers the Sun. They are different nuclear reactions.
misconceptions.remediation: Fix one fact to each word: fission SPLITS (used in reactors on Earth); fusion JOINS (powers the Sun).

common_mistakes.why: Both ideas are often praised together in everyday discussion of green energy.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Separate the two questions: does the resource replenish naturally (renewability), and what land, materials or ecosystem effects does it have (impact)? A resource can score well on one and poorly on the other.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming every power station must use a boiler and a steam turbine.
common_mistakes.why: The fossil-fuel, boiler-and-steam route is the example most commonly pictured first when 'generating electricity' is mentioned.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check whether the resource's energy arrives as heat (needing a boiler), as motion (turning a turbine directly), or as light (solar cells, no turbine at all).

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating nuclear fission and nuclear fusion as the same process.
common_mistakes.why: Both involve atomic nuclei and release very large amounts of energy, so the names can blur together.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Use a two-column comparison: fission splits a heavy nucleus and is used in current reactors; fusion joins light nuclei and powers stars.

exam_notes: When describing a generation route, name every store and pathway in order, from the original source to the final electrical output; a route description with a missing stage loses marks even if the overall idea is right.
A 'best resource' question almost always expects a comparison against stated criteria (availability, reliability, scale, renewability, environmental impact), not a single universal answer.
Keep nuclear fission (reactors on Earth) and nuclear fusion (the Sun) clearly separate in any answer that mentions either.

summary.big_idea: Every electricity-generating resource is a specific chain of energy stores and transfer pathways traced back to an original source, and comparing resources means weighing that chain against stated criteria, not naming one universal 'best' choice.
key_points: Most generation routes boil water to drive a steam turbine; hydroelectric dams, waves, tides and wind turn a turbine directly; solar cells generate electricity directly from light with no turbine at all, and a solar thermal collector only heats water, generating no electricity.
Renewable means replenished naturally on a human timescale, not impact-free.
Most resources trace back to the Sun; geothermal, nuclear and tidal are the stated exceptions.
Nuclear fission (splitting large nuclei, used in reactors) and nuclear fusion (joining small nuclei, powering the Sun) are different processes.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Before calling one resource 'the best', ask 'best by which criterion, for which situation?' — availability, reliability, scale, renewability and environmental impact can each point to a different answer.

summary.big_idea: Use the key physics ideas and methods from energy work and power accurately in mixed practice and exam-style problems.

exercises.statement: How much work is done when a mass of 3 kg (weighing 30 N) is lifted vertically through 6 m?
exercises.full_solution: Work done against gravity is given by $W = F \times d$, where $F$ is the force needed (here, the weight of the object) and $d$ is the distance moved in the direction of the force. The weight is given directly as 30 N, and the vertical distance lifted is 6 m, so $W = 30\,\text{N} \times 6\,\text{m} = 180\,\text{J}$. Note the mass of 3 kg is consistent with a weight of 30 N since $g = 10\,\text{N/kg}$ is used throughout these exercises, but it is not actually needed for the calculation because the weight is already given.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.361), Q1

exercises.statement: A hiker climbs a hill 300 m high. If she has a mass of 50 kg, calculate the work she does in lifting her body to the top of the hill.
exercises.full_solution: To lift her own weight up the hill, the hiker does work against gravity equal to $W = \text{weight} \times \text{height}$. Using $g = 10\,\text{N/kg}$ (the value used throughout these exercises), her weight is $50\,\text{kg} \times 10\,\text{N/kg} = 500\,\text{N}$. The work done in climbing the 300 m height is then $W = 500\,\text{N} \times 300\,\text{m} = 150\,000\,\text{J} = 150\,\text{kJ}$.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.361), Q2

exercises.statement: In loading a lorry a man lifts boxes each of weight 100 N through a height of 1.5 m. (a) How much work does he do in lifting one box? (b) How much energy is transferred when one box is lifted?
exercises.full_solution: (a) Work done = force $\times$ distance moved in the direction of the force. Here the force needed is the weight of the box, 100 N, and it is raised 1.5 m, so $W = 100\,\text{N} \times 1.5\,\text{m} = 150\,\text{J}$. (b) By the principle of conservation of energy, the work done on the box is exactly equal to the energy transferred to it (here, converted into gravitational potential energy as it is raised), so the energy transferred is also 150 J.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.361), Q3

exercises.statement: Name the energy transfers which occur when (a) an electric bell rings (b) someone speaks into a microphone (c) a ball is thrown upwards (d) there is a picture on a television screen (e) a torch is on.
exercises.answer:
Each device or event is simply an energy transfer from one store/form to another. (a) An electric bell uses electrical energy to move a hammer/striker (kinetic energy), which hits a gong and produces sound energy. (b) A microphone works in reverse to a loudspeaker: the sound energy of the voice vibrates a diaphragm, and this is converted into an electrical signal (electrical energy). (c) The muscles use chemical energy (ultimately from food) to give the ball kinetic energy as it leaves the hand; once in the air and rising, this kinetic energy is being transferred into gravitational potential energy as the ball slows and gains height. (d) A television screen converts the electrical energy supplied to it into light energy (the picture), with some energy inevitably wasted as heat. (e) In a torch, chemical energy stored in the battery is converted to electrical energy, which lights the bulb/LED, converting electrical energy into light energy (plus some unwanted heat).

**The same answers in syllabus wording (stores and pathways).** this course asks you to name the **store** the energy is in and the **pathway** by which it moves. (a) Energy is transferred electrically from the supply to the bell; some of it fills the kinetic store of the striker, and energy then leaves the gong as sound waves and by heating, so the internal (thermal) store of the surroundings increases. (b) Sound waves carry energy to the diaphragm, filling its kinetic store, and the microphone transfers that energy electrically along the cable. (c) The chemical store of the thrower's muscles empties while the hand does mechanical work on the ball, filling the ball's kinetic store; as the ball rises it does work against gravity, so energy moves from its kinetic store to the gravitational potential store. (d) Energy is transferred electrically to the screen, leaves it as light (waves), and the rest raises the internal (thermal) store of the set and the surrounding air by heating. (e) The chemical store of the battery empties, energy is transferred electrically to the bulb or LED, and leaves it both as light (waves) and by heating, so the internal (thermal) store of the surroundings increases.

exercises.statement: Name the forms of energy represented by the letters A, B, C and D in the following statement. In a coal-fired power station, the (A) energy of coal becomes (B) energy which changes water into steam. The steam drives a turbine which drives a generator. A generator transfers (C) energy into (D) energy.
exercises.answer:
Working through the chain of energy transfers in a coal-fired power station: coal is a fuel, so it stores (A) chemical energy. Burning the coal releases this as (B) heat energy, which boils water into steam. The expanding steam does work on the turbine blades, making them spin, so the turbine (and the generator shaft it turns) has (C) kinetic energy. Finally, the generator converts this kinetic energy of rotation into (D) electrical energy, which is sent out on the grid.

**The same chain in syllabus wording (stores and pathways).** A is the chemical store of the coal. Burning it transfers energy by heating into the internal (thermal) store of the water and steam, which is what B names. The steam then does mechanical work on the turbine blades, filling the kinetic store of the turbine and generator shaft, which is C. Finally the generator transfers energy electrically to the grid, which is what D names. Notice that B and C are stores but D is a pathway: 'electrical energy' is not a store in the GCSE list, so the careful statement is 'energy is transferred electrically', ending up in the stores of whatever the grid supplies.

exercises.statement: State what energy transfers occur in (a) a hairdryer (b) a refrigerator (c) an audio system.
exercises.answer:
(a) A hairdryer has two electrical components: a motor, which converts electrical energy into kinetic energy to drive the fan, and a heating element, which converts electrical energy into heat energy; together they blow heated air. (b) A refrigerator uses electrical energy to drive a compressor motor (kinetic energy), which pumps refrigerant around a circuit so as to extract heat energy from the food compartment and release it (as heat energy) at the back of the fridge — it does not create 'coldness', it moves heat energy out. (c) An audio system (amplifier and speakers) converts the electrical energy of the signal into sound energy, with some electrical energy inevitably wasted as heat in the components.

**The same answers in syllabus wording (stores and pathways).** (a) Energy is transferred electrically from the supply: a little fills the kinetic store of the fan, while most passes by heating into the internal (thermal) store of the element and then of the air blown out. (b) Energy is transferred electrically to the compressor, whose moving parts do mechanical work on the refrigerant; this allows energy to be transferred by heating out of the internal (thermal) store of the food and into the internal (thermal) store of the kitchen, which gains both that energy and the electrical input. (c) Energy is transferred electrically to the amplifier and speakers; the cones carry energy away as sound waves, and the rest raises the internal (thermal) store of the components and the surrounding air by heating.

exercises.statement: (a) When the energy input to a gas-fired power station is 1000 MJ, the electrical energy output is 300 MJ. What is the efficiency of the power station in changing the energy in gas into electrical energy? (b) What form does the 700 MJ of 'lost' energy take? (c) What is the fate of the 'lost' energy?
exercises.answer: (a) 30%. (b) Mainly heat (thermal) energy, with a small amount of sound energy. (c) It spreads out into the surroundings (e.g. via cooling towers, flue gases, and warm water) and is eventually dispersed into the wider environment, becoming too spread out to be usefully recovered.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Efficiency is the fraction of energy input that is converted into the useful output, as a percentage: $\text{efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}} \times 100\%$. Here, $\dfrac{300\,\text{MJ}}{1000\,\text{MJ}} \times 100\% = 30\%$. (b) By conservation of energy, the 'missing' $1000 - 300 = 700\,\text{MJ}$ has not disappeared — it has simply not been converted to the useful (electrical) form. In a power station this un-used energy mostly ends up as heat energy (warming the cooling water, exhaust gases and surroundings), plus a little as sound. (c) This heat energy spreads out into the power station's surroundings (air, river/sea water used for cooling, etc.) and ultimately disperses through the environment; once it is this spread out and at a low temperature it can no longer easily be used to do further useful work, even though the total quantity of energy is unchanged.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.364), Q7

exercises.statement: Calculate the kinetic energy of (a) a 1 kg trolley travelling at 2 m/s (b) a 2 g (0.002 kg) bullet travelling at 400 m/s (c) a 500 kg car travelling at 72 km/h.
exercises.full_solution: Kinetic energy is given by $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. (a) $KE = \tfrac12 \times 1\,\text{kg} \times (2\,\text{m/s})^2 = \tfrac12 \times 1 \times 4 = 2\,\text{J}$. (b) $KE = \tfrac12 \times 0.002\,\text{kg} \times (400\,\text{m/s})^2 = \tfrac12 \times 0.002 \times 160\,000 = 160\,\text{J}$. (c) First convert the speed to m/s: $72\,\text{km/h} = 72\,000\,\text{m} / 3600\,\text{s} = 20\,\text{m/s}$. Then $KE = \tfrac12 \times 500\,\text{kg} \times (20\,\text{m/s})^2 = \tfrac12 \times 500 \times 400 = 100\,000\,\text{J} = 100\,\text{kJ}$.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.364), Q8

exercises.statement: (a) What is the velocity of an object of mass 1 kg which has 200 J of kinetic energy? (b) Calculate the gravitational potential energy of a 5 kg mass when it is (i) 3 m (ii) 6 m above the ground. ($g = 10\,\text{N/kg}$.)
exercises.full_solution: (a) Rearranging $KE = \tfrac12 mv^2$ for $v$ gives $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times KE}{m}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 200\,\text{J}}{1\,\text{kg}}} = \sqrt{400} = 20\,\text{m/s}$. (b) Gravitational potential energy is $PE = mgh$, with $m = 5\,\text{kg}$ and $g = 10\,\text{N/kg}$. (i) At $h = 3\,\text{m}$: $PE = 5 \times 10 \times 3 = 150\,\text{J}$. (ii) At $h = 6\,\text{m}$: $PE = 5 \times 10 \times 6 = 300\,\text{J}$. As expected, doubling the height exactly doubles the potential energy, since $PE$ is directly proportional to $h$.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.364), Q9

exercises.statement: A boy whose weight is 600 N runs up a flight of stairs 10 m high in 12 s. What is his average power?
exercises.full_solution: Power is the rate of doing work, $P = \dfrac{W}{t}$. The work done against gravity in climbing the stairs is $W = \text{weight} \times \text{height} = 600\,\text{N} \times 10\,\text{m} = 6000\,\text{J}$. His average power is then $P = \dfrac{6000\,\text{J}}{12\,\text{s}} = 500\,\text{W}$.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.365), Q10

exercises.statement: An escalator carries 60 people of average mass 70 kg to a height of 5 m in one minute. Find the power needed to do this.
exercises.full_solution: First find the total mass carried: $60 \times 70\,\text{kg} = 4200\,\text{kg}$. Using $g = 10\,\text{N/kg}$, the total weight is $4200 \times 10 = 42\,000\,\text{N}$. The work done in raising this weight through 5 m is $W = 42\,000\,\text{N} \times 5\,\text{m} = 210\,000\,\text{J}$. Since this happens over one minute, $t = 60\,\text{s}$, the power needed is $P = \dfrac{210\,000\,\text{J}}{60\,\text{s}} = 3500\,\text{W} = 3.5\,\text{kW}$.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.365), Q11

exercises.statement: The pie chart in the supplied diagram shows the percentages of the main energy sources used by a certain country: oil 40%, natural gas 25%, coal 25%, nuclear 8%, water 2%. (a) What percentage is supplied by water power? (b) Which of the sources is/are renewable? (c) What is meant by 'renewable'? (d) Name two other renewable sources. (e) Why, if energy is always conserved, is it important to develop renewable sources?
exercises.answer: (a) 2%. (b) Water (hydroelectric) power only. (c) A renewable energy source is one that is naturally replenished (e.g. by sunlight, the water cycle, wind, or the tides) at least as fast as it is used, so it does not get permanently used up. (d) e.g. wind and solar (also acceptable: tidal, geothermal, biomass/biofuels). (e) Although the total amount of energy is conserved, each time energy is transferred some of it becomes spread out as low-grade heat that can no longer be usefully recovered to do work; fossil and nuclear fuels are finite stores that are being used up and their burning causes pollution and climate change, so renewable sources (continually replenished and generally cleaner) must be developed to keep supplying useful energy into the future.
exercises.full_solution: (a) Reading the pie chart directly, the water (hydroelectric) slice is labelled 2%. As a check, the five percentages given (oil 40%, gas 25%, coal 25%, nuclear 8%, water 2%) sum to $40+25+25+8+2=100\%$, confirming the chart is self-consistent. (b) Of oil, gas, coal, nuclear and water, only water (hydroelectric) power is renewable — oil, gas and coal are fossil fuels (finite underground stores) and nuclear fuel (uranium) is also a finite mined resource, whereas flowing/falling water is continually replenished by the water cycle, which is driven by the Sun. (c) 'Renewable' means the source is naturally and continuously replenished (for example by sunlight, wind, or the water cycle) at a rate comparable to how fast it is used, so unlike fossil fuels it cannot be exhausted or 'run out' on a human timescale. (d) Other renewable sources include wind energy (wind turbines), solar energy (solar cells/panels), tidal energy, geothermal energy and biofuels/biomass; any two of these are acceptable. (e) Energy is indeed always conserved overall, but each energy transfer tends to degrade some of the useful (concentrated) energy into heat that spreads out into the surroundings and becomes too dilute to do further useful work — this is why we cannot simply keep reusing the same energy. Non-renewable sources (fossil fuels, nuclear fuel) exist in limited quantities and are being depleted, and burning fossil fuels also releases pollutants and greenhouse gases. Renewable sources are continually replenished (ultimately mostly by the Sun) and generally have a smaller environmental impact, so developing them is essential for a continued, sustainable supply of useful energy.
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.369), Q12

exercises.statement: List six properties which you think the ideal energy source should have for generating electricity in a power station.
exercises.answer: For example: (1) it should be renewable / never run out; (2) it should be cheap to build the power station and to run/fuel; (3) it should produce little or no pollution or greenhouse gas emissions; (4) it should be reliable, able to supply electricity on demand at any time regardless of weather or season; (5) it should have a short start-up time so output can be matched quickly to changing demand; (6) it should be safe, both in normal operation and in the disposal/decommissioning of waste and plant.
exercises.full_solution: This is an open-ended, discuss-and-list question, so any six sensible, justified properties should be credited. Drawing on the economic, environmental and reliability factors discussed for different energy sources (cost per unit of electricity, start-up time, reliability, and pollution), a good set of six properties for an 'ideal' source is: it should be renewable (does not get used up); it should be cheap, both to build the generating plant and to operate per unit of electricity produced; it should produce minimal pollution or greenhouse gases; it should be reliable and available at any time of day or year, independent of weather; it should have a short start-up time, so supply can be adjusted quickly to meet changing demand; and it should be safe to operate and to decommission, with no hazardous waste. (Other acceptable answers include: high energy output/efficiency, limited land/space use, and ease of transport or storage of the fuel.)
exercises.source_label: P2 Work, Energy and Power — Questions (p.369), Q13
